**Monday, August 24, 1931**

The date has witnessed destruction before. On August 24, 1814 — 117 years before your birth, to the day — British forces entered Washington D.C. and burned it. The White House was set alight; the Capitol's interior was gutted; the Library of Congress lost its collection. Dolley Madison rescued a portrait of George Washington before fleeing the city. A violent rainstorm extinguished the fires overnight, the British withdrew, and the city was rebuilt. For one August 24, the capital of the American republic had been reduced to ash and rubble.

On August 24, 79 AD — 1,852 years before your birth — Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii. The younger Pliny watched from across the bay. August 24 has a history of catastrophe and reconstitution.

The catastrophe that coincided with your actual arrival was quieter in form but significant in consequence. On August 24, 1931, the government of the United Kingdom dissolved and reformed itself in a single day. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald — a Labour leader — broke with his own party and reconstituted his cabinet as a National Government coalition with the Conservatives and Liberals. The financial crisis had grown severe enough that the pound itself was under threat, gold reserves draining, and MacDonald's Labour cabinet had refused to accept the austerity required to stabilize them. He chose the country over his party. Labour expelled him immediately. He remained prime minister, leading a government mostly composed of his political opponents, and was finished as a Labour figure for the rest of his life. The child born that Monday arrived on the day a major political career ended in the service of institutional survival.

The world producing that crisis was the world you were born into. The Great Depression had been running for nearly two years. Germany's Danat Bank had collapsed in July, sending shockwaves through the European financial system. One in five Americans was unemployed. Banks across the United States were failing at a rate of hundreds per year. Soup kitchens and breadlines were ordinary features of city life. The economic confidence of the 1920s had not merely stumbled — it had shattered, and no one knew what would follow.

What followed, in Germany, was answer enough. Adolf Hitler's party had become the second largest in the Reichstag in September 1930, riding Depression-era desperation into mass support. In August 1931, he was not yet chancellor — that came in January 1933. But the machinery was already running. The child born on August 24, 1931, spent the first conscious years of life watching it arrive.

**Twenty-five days after your birth** — on September 18, 1931 — Japanese officers staged an explosion on a Manchurian railroad and used it as pretext to invade. It was the first deliberate step toward the Second World War. You would be ten years old when Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and fourteen when the war ended — in the summer of 1945, the same summer the atomic bomb destroyed two cities and the world learned what it had built.

You were thirteen when Hiroshima happened. You were fourteen when it was over. The nuclear age — its weapons, its deterrence, its existential dread — began in your adolescence. You have lived the entire span of it in one lifetime.

Now here is an exact-date connection that falls on your birthday itself. On **August 24, 1954** — your twenty-third birthday — President Eisenhower signed the Communist Control Act, effectively outlawing the Communist Party from American political life. The McCarthy era was at its height; loyalty investigations were consuming careers and reputations. The act passed a Congress that barely debated it, so complete was the climate of fear. You turned twenty-three on the day the United States codified into law what its inquisitors had been practicing for years. You were old enough to understand precisely what that meant, and young enough that it shaped the political consciousness you carried forward.

Consider the full distance of ninety-five years. You were born before commercial television, before radar, before jet aviation, before penicillin was in widespread use. Three months before your birth, the Empire State Building had been completed; it was the tallest structure in the world, and radio was how millions of people learned this. Charles Lindbergh had crossed the Atlantic just four years earlier. FDR's fireside chats — a president speaking with intimacy directly to millions — still lay ahead.

In ninety-five years: the New Deal; the Second World War; the Holocaust laid bare at Nuremberg; the full arc of the Cold War from Hiroshima to the Berlin Wall; Korea; the Civil Rights movement; the Moon; Nixon's fall; the personal computer; AIDS; the Soviet Union's collapse; the internet; 9/11; a global pandemic; and now an AI revolution that is changing how human beings write, think, and know things.

The Washington D.C. that burned on August 24, 1814 was rebuilt within a few years — more permanent, more convinced of its own continuity. The world of August 24, 1931 has been destroyed and rebuilt several times since, each time less certain of permanence than before. You have been present for every demolition and every reconstruction. That is what ninety-five years contains: not merely time, but the accumulated evidence that nothing believed to be fixed ever quite is.
